Data redundancy

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Backups create recoverable copies of data or systems so organizations can restore after deletion, corruption, ransomware, or disaster. Good backup strategy considers location, frequency, retention, immutability, encryption, and restore testing.
course.why: A backup is valuable only if it survives the incident and can actually be restored within business requirements.
course.example: An organization keeps frequent local backups for speed plus protected offsite/immutable copies so ransomware cannot destroy every recovery point.
course.exam: Know onsite vs offsite, snapshots vs true backups, restore testing, and the fact that replication does not replace historical backup copies.

breakdown.explanation: Use duplicate components or paths so one failure does not stop the service.

slides.title: Encryption
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.
defs: Transforms readable plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key so unauthorized parties cannot understand it.

course.learn: Encryption converts plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key so unauthorized parties cannot understand the data. Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret; asymmetric encryption uses a public/private key pair.
course.why: Encryption is one of the primary ways to protect confidentiality for data at rest and in transit.
course.example: A laptop uses full-disk encryption, while a TLS session protects web traffic crossing an untrusted network.
course.exam: Encryption = confidentiality and reversible with the correct key. Hashing is one-way and primarily supports integrity.

slides.title: Snapshots
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: A snapshot captures the state of a system, volume, or virtual machine at a point in time so changes can be rolled back or compared later.
course.why: Snapshots can make short-term recovery fast, but they may depend on the same storage and therefore are not automatically independent backups.
course.example: Before a risky software upgrade, an administrator takes a VM snapshot and reverts when the upgrade fails.
course.exam: Snapshot ≠ guaranteed backup. Ask whether it is independent, protected, and retained appropriately.

slides.title: Replication
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.
defs: Ensuring authorized users can access systems and data when needed.

course.learn: Replication copies data or system state to another location, often continuously or frequently, to improve availability and recovery speed.
course.why: Replication can also copy corruption, deletion, or ransomware changes, so historical backups are still necessary.
course.example: A database streams changes to a secondary region that can become active after a regional outage.
course.exam: Replication = availability/current copy. Backup = recoverable historical copy.

breakdown.explanation: High availability designs services to remain accessible despite failures. It uses redundancy, failover, load balancing, clustering, replication, resilient power, and removal of single points of failure.

slides.title: Journaling
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Journaling records changes or transactions in a log before or alongside applying them to the main data structure. It can help reconstruct a consistent state after interruption.
course.why: A journal provides a history of recent operations that supports recovery and investigation.
course.example: A file system replays its journal after an unexpected shutdown to complete or roll back incomplete operations.
course.exam: Journal = record of changes/transactions; it complements backups and replication.
